item.title: Kicksecure 18: emerg-shutdown causes immediate power-off during boot after LUKS unlock
item.dc:creator: SpecialBook
item.description:
# Kicksecure 18: emerg-shutdown causes immediate power-off during boot after LUKS unlock

Environment

  • OS: Kicksecure 18, bare metal, LXQt
  • Kernel: `6.12.113+deb13-amd64`
  • Package: `security-misc-shared 3:54.2-1`
  • Storage: Internal NVMe SSD
  • Root filesystem: ext4 on LUKS encryption
  • Initramfs: dracut
  • Hardware: Lenovo laptop, AMD platform

Problem

After entering the LUKS passphrase during a normal boot, the computer abruptly powers off before reaching the login screen.

The issue is reproducible whenever `emerg-shutdown.service` is enabled.

Booting with the following temporary kernel parameters allows the system to start normally:

```text
systemd.mask=emerg-shutdown.service rd.systemd.mask=emerg-shutdown.service
```

No shutdown reason or kernel panic is visible in the journal.

Steps to reproduce

  1. Enable `emerg-shutdown.service`.
  2. Reboot normally.
  3. Enter the LUKS passphrase.
  4. The system proceeds into normal systemd initialization.
  5. `emerg-shutdown.service` starts.
  6. The computer abruptly powers off.

Troubleshooting performed

**1. Recovery mode**

Booting into single-user recovery mode and then running `exit` allowed the system to continue booting successfully.

Booting directly into `multi-user.target` did not resolve the problem.

**2. Disabling emerg-shutdown**

Masking `emerg-shutdown.service` during boot prevents the unexpected power-off.

**4. Testing without boot-device monitoring**

Created a temporary systemd override replacing `ExecStart` with:

```ini
[Service]
Type=simple
ExecStart=
ExecStart=/usr/bin/emerg-shutdown --keys=KEY_LEFTCTRL|KEY_RIGHTCTRL,KEY_LEFTALT|KEY_RIGHTALT,KEY_END
```

the system again powered off during boot.

This suggests that monitoring the NVMe device is not required to reproduce the issue. However, the binary still initializes and processes Netlink events even when `–devices` is omitted.

**5. NVMe and USBGuard**

The root-device detection helper correctly resolves the encrypted root filesystem to its underlying NVMe partition.

Available kernel logs show normal NVMe detection and filesystem mounting, without obvious device disconnection or I/O errors.

USBGuard logs show permitted devices and no obvious blocking event associated with the issue.

Relevant logs

From an unsuccessful boot:

```text
systemd[1]: Starting emerg-shutdown.service - Emergency shutdown when boot media is removed…
emerg-shutdown: path: /
emerg-shutdown: is block device: no
emerg-shutdown: path: /dev/mapper/[REDACTED_LUKS_DEVICE]
emerg-shutdown: is block device: yes
emerg-shutdown: real_dev_path: /dev/dm-0
emerg-shutdown: path: /dev/dm-0
emerg-shutdown: is block device: yes
emerg-shutdown: dm slaves_dir: /sys/class/block/dm-0/slaves
emerg-shutdown: path: /dev/nvme0n1p5
emerg-shutdown: is block device: yes
systemd[1]: Started emerg-shutdown.service - Emergency shutdown when boot media is removed.
```

In a separate failed boot with the keyboard-only override:

```text
systemd[1]: Started emerg-shutdown.service - Emergency shutdown when boot media is removed.
```

The system then powered off unexpectedly. No clear reason was recorded.

The journal excerpts are selected from different failed boots. Identifying values and timestamps have been removed.

Expected behavior

`emerg-shutdown` should remain enabled and permit normal system boot unless the configured emergency key combination is pressed or a monitored boot device is actually removed.

Questions

  1. Is this a known issue with `security-misc-shared 3:54.2-1`?
  2. Is there a recommended fix that preserves the emergency keyboard shortcut rather than disabling the service entirely?

I would prefer to keep the emergency shutdown functionality enabled.

Thank you.

4 posts - 2 participants

Read full topic
item.source: Kicksecure 18: emerg-shutdown causes immediate power-off during boot after LUKS unlock

item.title: Kicksecure 18.2.4.2 - Point Release!
item.dc:creator: Patrick
item.description:
Download

Kicksecure – 25 Dec 25

Download Kicksecure (FREE)

FREE download of Kicksecure. Kicksecure can be installed on a physical machine as the host operating system (OS), as a guest OS inside a virtual machine, or as a portable host OS on a USB data stick.

(What is a point release?)

Upgrade

Alternatively, an in-place release upgrade is possible using the Kicksecure repository.

This release would not have been possible without the numerous supporters of Kicksecure!

Please Donate!

Kicksecure – 25 Dec 25

Donating to Kicksecure

PayPal, Bitcoin (BTC), Monero (XMR), Ethereum (ETH) or Token, Credit Card, Bank Wire, Others

Please Contribute!

Kicksecure – 29 Apr 26

Contribute to Kicksecure

Spread, Follow, Develop, Testing, Donate. Contribute to Freedom Software / Open Source.

Security Vulnerability Fixes

  • Fixed a local privilege escalation vulnerability in a script in the legacy-dist package. (Thanks to Uladzislau Hryharovich for responsibly disclosing this security vulnerability!)
    • (The fixed legacy-dist package was already available in the stable repository before this release announcement.)
    • A full write-up by the reporter will be linked here once published.
      • EDIT: #cybersecurity #infosec #vulnerability #vulnerabilityresearch #responsibledisclosure #linux | Uladzislau Hryharovich

Major Changes

  • Ported the ISO build process from live-build (run through derivative-maker) to native derivative-maker (without live-build).
  • Progress towards reproducible builds.
    • Packages built by Kicksecure are already reproducible. Independent reproduction of packages and comparison of official builds with reproduced builds are welcome so that potential issues can be identified and resolved.
    • Non-Qubes-Whonix: the next release might be reproducible.
    • (Qubes-Whonix: reproducibility depends on Qubes, not Qubes-Whonix.)
  • Internal code review and fixes.
  • Major progress on automated testing.
  • derivative-maker: opt-in, disabled-by-default SMBIOS reader that allows kernel parameters to be configured at the virtualizer level.

Notable Changes

  • desktop-config-dist:
    • Removed the QTerminal drop-down keybinding.
    • Ported livecheck to Qt6; added D-Bus activation to launch new instances from the Start Menu.
    • Restricted livecheck to one running instance at a time; the Start Menu entry now raises the existing livecheck window.
    • Hidden the gparted Start Menu entry in user sessions by default (non-functional due to user-sysmaint-split).
  • developer-meta-files (build and maintenance tooling):
    • dm-review-branch: review changes on a git branch before merging.
    • dm-reproducible-compare-artifacts: compare two builds artifact-by-artifact to verify that they are identical.
    • dm-nbd-cleanup: clean up leftover block devices after a build.
    • bash-style-guide: project coding style guide for shell scripts.
    • dm-reproducible-buildinfo: record the exact build inputs needed to reproduce a build.
    • dm-reproducible-fetch: fetch build sources deterministically so everyone starts with the same inputs.
    • dm-reproducible-verify: rebuild and verify that the result matches the official release bit-for-bit.
    • dm-normalize-fat-partition: remove nondeterministic FAT filesystem metadata to make images reproducible.
    • dm-debconf-normalize-owners: normalize debconf database ownership for reproducible packaging.
    • dm-update-frozen-snapshot: update the pinned package repository snapshot used by the build.
    • dm-github-org-security-report: collect open security alerts across the GitHub organization.
    • dm-github-org-policy: apply a standard security policy across the GitHub organization’s repositories.
  • dist-system-metadata:
    • New dist-system-metadata package.
      System metadata has been split out of tb-updater so that frequently changing
      data (pinned Tor Browser versions and the Tor Project signing key) can
      migrate between suites independently of the larger code packages.
      • usr/share/dist-system-metadata/tb-updater/{tbb_hardcoded_version_stable,
        tbb_hardcoded_version_alpha,tbb-team.asc}
      • Minimal dependencies allow it to migrate to the stable repository quickly.
  • helper-scripts:
    • dpkg-reconfigure-noninteractive: reconfigure a package without interactive prompts.
    • Fixed qubes-dom0-update over sys-whonix.
      Can't update dom0 over sys-whonix in QubesOS - Qubes-Whonix - Whonix Forum
    • check-ref-commits: check git commit references for validity.
    • lockfile.sh: simple file-locking helper to prevent concurrent runs (to be renamed to lockfile.bsh).
    • detect-software-rendering: detect whether the GPU is using software (CPU) rendering.
    • vbox-ova-reproducible-normalize: normalize a VirtualBox .ova for reproducible builds.
  • GRUB:
    • Theme: pin the theme variant instead of detecting the build host’s firmware, improving reproducibility.
    • Improved support for /boot (symlinks, FAT32), with further improvements planned for the next version.
  • live-config-dist:
    • argument-squashfs-pack: build an optional compressed (squashfs) filesystem for a live system to be installed by the Calamares installer. (Development tool)
    • persistence-setup: set up persistent storage for live systems. (Development tool)
    • mok-enroll-opt-in: enable opt-in Secure Boot key (MOK) enrollment via the MOK_ENROLL=1 environment variable. (Development tool)
  • security-misc:
    • SSH client and server configuration: restricted key exchange to post-quantum algorithms.
  • usability-misc:
    • console-setup: run only when a framebuffer is available (skip on serial/headless systems).
      On a headless or serial-only boot (no GPU and therefore no /dev/fb0), setupcon’s setfont
      cannot work and repeatedly logs ‘setfont: ERROR ioctl(KDFONTOP): Invalid argument’
      in the journal. The console-setup.service drop-in is now gated by
      ConditionPathExists=/dev/fb0, allowing it to be skipped cleanly in these environments.
      Normal graphical boots have /dev/fb0 and remain unaffected.
  • vm-config-dist:
    • Improved detection of whether software rendering is enabled.

Full difference of all changes

item.title: Random log outs, amd_pstate failed to load, keyring mismatch, and more!
item.dc:creator: sublime.dust
item.description:
I installed Kicksecure on my desktop yesterday, and since then I have spent several hours attempting to debug it, with limited success.

I am at my wits end.

After my initial install, I was experiencing many of these problems (random logouts, amd_pstate failed to load, kanshi config not applied automatically) and then the terminal suddenly stopped working. When I tried to open Qterminal or use anything in the System Maintenance Panel that would normally launch the Qterminal, nothing happened.

I could not find any way to fix this or install another terminal emulator, so I reinstalled the system from scratch. My terminal is back, but there are several other problems.

I considered creating a separate post for each of these, but it seems likely that at least some of these issues are connected. I’m using the latest version of Kicksecure, based on Debian 13.6.

Overview of Problems:

  1. Logged out of computer at random intervals
  2. Kanshi config is not automatically applied upon startup
  3. amd_pstate failed to load
  4. sudo apt update: Error due to keyring mismatch
  5. systemd critical journal messages - nouveau, channel 16 killed

1. Logged out of computer at random intervals

At seemingly random intervals, I am logged out of the computer and end up on the black log in screen where it asks me to enter my username. When I log back in, all of my applications are closed and anything I didn’t save is gone. This has happened while I am actively using my computer, and it has happened twice while writing this post. This could be coincidental, but it only seems to happen when I have adjusted the scale of my display.

2. Kanshi config is not automatically applied upon startup

When I restart Kanshi the settings in my config file are applied, but I have to do that manually every single time I boot my computer. I tried to get around this by creating the file /etc/rc.local with the following contents and giving it execute permissions. This script is supposed to run on start up, but my display config settings are only applied if I execute the script manually.

#!/bin/sh

systemctl --user restart kanshi

exit 0

3. amd_pstate failed to load

Every time I boot my computer, before I enter the passphrase to decrypt my drive, it outputs:

[    5.447055] amd_pstate: failed to enable driver mode(3)

When I run lsmod it does not list amd_pstate. When I run modprobe, it outputs:

[user ~]% sudo modprobe amd_pstate
modprobe: FATAL: Module amd_pstate not found in directory /lib/modules/6.12.111+deb13-amd64

item.title: Ledger Nano S+ (2c97:5000) rejected by USBGuard rule 39 on hotplug — reboot makes it work
item.dc:creator: kick
item.description:
Hi,

I’m running Debian 13 (Trixie) with Kicksecure hardening on bare metal, and I’m troubleshooting a Ledger Nano S+ USB authorization problem.

The Ledger itself is working correctly. I have tested two different Nano S+ devices, two original Ledger USB cables, and three different USB ports.

The interesting part is that the kernel detects the Ledger correctly, but USBGuard rejects it.

USBGuard configuration

USBGuard is active:

usbguard.service - USBGuard daemon
Active: active (running)

The kernel USB authorization default is:

$ cat /sys/module/usbcore/parameters/authorized_default
1

USBGuard is configured with:

$ sudo usbguard get-parameter ImplicitPolicyTarget
block

So the default policy is to block unknown USB devices.

Ledger detection

When I plug in the Ledger, dmesg shows:

usb 1-2: new full-speed USB device number 5 using xhci_hcd
usb 1-2: New USB device found, idVendor=2c97, idProduct=5000, bcdDevice= 2.01
usb 1-2: New USB device strings: Mfr=1, Product=2, SerialNumber=3
usb 1-2: Product: Nano S+
usb 1-2: Manufacturer: Ledger
usb 1-2: SerialNumber: 0001
usb 1-2: Device is not authorized for usage
usb 1-2: USB disconnect, device number 5

The same happens on a second connection attempt.

USBGuard watch shows the reason

Running:

sudo usbguard watch

produces:

[device] PresenceChanged: id=63
 event=Insert
 target=block
 device_rule=block id 2c97:5000 serial "0001" name "Nano S+"
 ...
 with-interface { 03:00:00 ff:ff:ff 03:01:01 }

[device] PolicyChanged: id=63
 target_old=block
 target_new=reject
 ...
 rule_id=39

[device] PolicyApplied: id=63
 target_new=reject
 ...
 rule_id=39

[device] PresenceChanged: id=63
 event=Remove
 target=reject

I then checked the actual USBGuard policy:

$ sudo usbguard list-rules | nl -ba | sed -n '35,42p'

35  35: reject with-interface all-of { 03:*:* dc:*:* }
36  36: reject with-interface all-of { 03:*:* e0:*:* }
37  37: reject with-interface all-of { 03:*:* ef:*:* }
38  38: reject with-interface all-of { 03:*:* fe:*:* }
39  39: reject with-interface all-of { 03:*:* ff:*:* }
40  40: reject with-interface one-of { ef:04:* }
41  41: allow with-interface 03:01:01 if !allowed-matches(with-interface equals { 03:01:01 })
42  42: allow with-interface 03:01:02 if !allowed-matches(with-interface equals { 03:01:02 })

The Ledger reports these interfaces:

{ 03:00:00 ff:ff:ff 03:01:01 }

Therefore rule 39 appears to match the Ledger because of:

ff:ff:ff

and USBGuard changes the device from block to reject.

The kernel then reports:

Device is not authorized for usage

and disconnects it.

However, rebooting changes the situation

I discovered an interesting workaround.

If I connect the Ledger, enter the PIN, and then reboot the system, after reboot the Nano can become available.

In the working state:

$ lsusb | grep -i -E 'ledger|2c97'
Bus 001 Device 002: ID 2c97:5000 Ledger Nano S+

and USBGuard shows:

55: allow id 2c97:5000 serial "0001" name "Nano S+"
    ...
    via-port "1-2"
    with-interface { 03:00:00 ff:ff:ff 03:01:01 }

Ledger Live then recognizes the device and I have verified the backup.

Interestingly, ImplicitPolicyTarget is still:

block

so I am not using ImplicitPolicyTarget=allow as a permanent workaround.

I also tested temporarily setting:

sudo usbguard set-parameter ImplicitPolicyTarget allow

but I don’t want to weaken the USB security policy just to make the Ledger work.

Question

Could someone explain the intended USBGuard/Kicksecure configuration for a Ledger Nano S+ in this situation?

Specifically:

  1. Is rule 39 (reject with-interface ... ff:*:*) expected to reject the Ledger’s ff:ff:ff interface?
  2. Should there be a Ledger-specific exception that takes precedence over this rule?
  3. Why does a reboot allow the Ledger to become usable despite the same generic reject rule being present?
  4. What is the recommended way under Kicksecure to permanently allow this specific Ledger while keeping:
ImplicitPolicyTarget=block

?

I would prefer not to remove rule 39 globally, since it appears to be a security rule for a reason.

Thanks!

Note: This investigation and forum post were prepared with assistance from ChatGPT.

7 posts - 3 participants

Read full topic
